raw_case_text:
A 5-year-old male patient was admitted to Children Medical Center (CMC) with inflammation and swelling in his left mandible and wrist without a history of trauma. In the past, he had suffered from several episodes of pneumonia which started at the age of seven months. On admission, laboratory findings included erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 84 mm/h, WBC count 12100/mm3 (61% neutrophils, 39% lymphocytes), hemoglobin 11.3 gr/dl and thrombocyte 386000/mm3. As the CRP analysis displayed 20 mg/dl, cephalexin (150 mg/kg/day) was initiated. In his roentgenogram, osteolytic lesions in the distal metaphase of hand and maxillary bone were observed. Considering history of several infections and multifocal osteomyelitis, bone biopsy was performed and his immune system function was evaluated. In the bone biopsy, non-necrotizing granulomatoid lesions were seen. The induration of purified protein derivative reaction was 10 mm diameter. Besides, HIV, hepatitis B surface antigen (HBs), rheumatoid factor and brucella agglutination tests were all negative. The serum IgG level was 1650 mg/dl (normal: 441-1135 mg/dl). IgM and IgA were in high normal range at 250 and 175 mg/dl, respectively. Because no defect was found in his humeral and cellular immunity, the phagocytic cells function was tested with a nitroblue-tetrazolium (NBT) slide test. Based on his hematological and immunological tests (NBT = 0), CGD was considered as underlying disease in this case. Regarding his NBT test, antibiotic therapy was changed from cephalexin to co-trimoxazole (20 mg/kg/day, iv) plus (along with) interferon-gamma (50 microgram/m2 every other day). After two weeks of treatment, the patient's condition improved and he was discharged with prescription of both cephalexin (100 mg/kg/day) and co-trimoxazole (10 mg/kg/day) to be taken orally as prophylaxis.
The patient was readmitted to our center after eight months with a tender mass in his right upper quadrant (RUQ) (Fig 1). On admission, his major complaint was severe dyspnea, a persistent cough and also chest and abdominal pain in epigastric area which was started 10 days ago. He was placed on antibiotic therapy including cephalexin (100 mg/kg/day). A computerized tomography (CT) scan of the chest and abdomen was performed which revealed the hypodense area in liver (Fig 2). Adjacent to this opacity, involvement of lower right ribs and reaction to soft tissue were also observed, indicating ribs osteomyelitis. After sonography guided drainage of the above-mentioned hepatic abscess, a sample was sent to the Mycology Department in Tehran University of Medical Sciences. The microscopic examination of clarified specimen with KOH 10% indicated the branched, septated and dichotomous mycelia (Fig. 3). The remaining specimen was also cultured on Brain Heart Infusion agar (BHI), Sabouraud's dextrose agar (S) and Sabouraud's containing 0.005% chloramphenicol (Sc). The S and Sc culture media were incubated at 25 C and BHI at 37 C. The colonies grew rapidly, attaining the diameter of 5 cm within 5 days and their color was bluish green. Cellophane tape preparations and slide cultures demonstrated septated, branched and hyaline hyphae with rough-walled conidiophores and radiated conidial heads. Based on these microscopic and macroscopic findings, Aspergillus fumigatus was determined as causative agent in this case. Deoxycholate Amphotericin B (1 mg/kg/day, iv), interferon-gamma (50 microgeram/m2 every other day, sc) and rifampicin (10 mg/kg/day) were administered with diagnosis of invasive aspergillosis. The only adverse event observed during treatment was hypokalemia, which was adjusted by administration of potassium chloride 15%. One month after initiation of antifungal therapy, his follow-up CT scan of the abdominal and thoracal region demonstrated relative resolution of hepatic abscess. After four weeks of intravenous treatment, the patient's clinical condition improved. He was discharged upon his parents' responsibility while continuing taking rifampicin (10 mg/kg/day) for two more weeks as a treatment in addition to co-trimoxazole (5 mg/kg/day) and itraconazole (4 mg/kg/day) as long term prophylaxis.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 5-year-old boy presented with atraumatic swelling and inflammation of the left mandible and wrist, followed 8 months later by a 10-day history of severe dyspnea, persistent cough, epigastric/chest pain, and a tender right upper quadrant mass.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 5-year-old boy with recurrent pneumonias since 7 months of age initially presented with atraumatic osteomyelitis of the left mandible/maxilla and distal hand metaphysis, leading to a diagnosis of chronic granulomatous disease (CGD). Eight months after discharge on prophylactic cephalexin and cotrimoxazole, he was readmitted with 10 days of severe dyspnea, persistent cough, chest and epigastric pain, and a tender right upper quadrant abdominal mass.
subjective.past_medical_history: Multiple episodes of pneumonia starting at 7 months of age; diagnosed with chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) at age 5 and maintained on oral prophylaxis with cephalexin (100 mg/kg/day) and cotrimoxazole (10 mg/kg/day).
subjective.review_of_systems: Initial admission: left mandibular and wrist pain and swelling. Readmission (8 months later): severe dyspnea, persistent cough, chest and epigastric pain, and right upper quadrant mass.

objective.physical_examination: Initial admission: inflammation and swelling over the left mandible and wrist. Readmission (8 months later): severe respiratory distress/dyspnea and a tender palpable mass in the right upper quadrant of the abdomen.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial admission: ESR 84 mm/h, WBC 12,100/mm3 (61% neutrophils, 39% lymphocytes), Hb 11.3 g/dL, platelets 386,000/mm3, CRP 20 mg/dL; serum IgG 1,650 mg/dL (normal: 441-1,135), IgM 250 mg/dL, IgA 175 mg/dL; PPD induration 10 mm; negative HIV, HBsAg, RF, and Brucella agglutination tests. Hand and facial radiographs showed osteolytic lesions in the distal hand metaphysis and maxillary/mandibular bone.
objective.advanced_workup: Initial bone biopsy showed non-necrotizing granulomatous osteomyelitis, and nitroblue tetrazolium (NBT) slide test was 0%, confirming chronic granulomatous disease (CGD). At readmission 8 months later, chest and abdominal CT demonstrated a hypodense hepatic abscess with contiguous osteomyelitis of the lower right ribs and soft-tissue reaction. Ultrasound-guided hepatic abscess aspiration KOH (10%) microscopy revealed dichotomously branching septate hyphae, and fungal cultures on Sabouraud dextrose and Brain Heart Infusion agar grew bluish-green colonies of Aspergillus fumigatus within 5 days.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Zero nitroblue tetrazolium reduction (NBT = 0) confirmed underlying chronic granulomatous disease (CGD, with brucellosis excluded), and mycological microscopy and culture of the drained hepatic abscess at 8-month readmission confirmed invasive Aspergillus fumigatus hepatic abscess and contiguous right rib osteomyelitis. Initial multifocal osteomyelitis responded to 2 weeks of IV cotrimoxazole (20 mg/kg/day) and subcutaneous interferon-gamma (50 ug/m2 every other day); the subsequent Aspergillus fumigatus hepatic abscess and rib osteomyelitis were treated with ultrasound-guided drainage, 4 weeks of IV deoxycholate amphotericin B (1 mg/kg/day, with KCl supplementation for hypokalemia), SC interferon-gamma (50 ug/m2 q48h), and oral rifampicin (10 mg/kg/day), followed by discharge on long-term oral itraconazole (4 mg/kg/day) and cotrimoxazole (5 mg/kg/day) prophylaxis after CT confirmed abscess resolution.
